theory.intro: **Blood alcohol content (BAC)** measures the mass of alcohol in grams per $100\text{ mL}$ of blood. It depends on sex, body mass ($M\text{ kg}$), standard drinks consumed ($N$), and drinking time ($H\text{ hours}$).
facts: $\text{BAC}_{\text{male}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$, where $N$ is standard drinks, $H$ is hours, and $M$ is mass in kilograms.
$\text{BAC}_{\text{female}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{5.5M}$, where $5.5$ reflects a lower average body water content in females than males ($6.8$).
Each standard drink has $10\text{ g}$ of alcohol ($10N$), and the body metabolises alcohol at $7.5\text{ g}$ per hour ($-7.5H$).
Learner and provisional drivers must maintain a zero BAC ($0.00$), while unrestricted drivers must stay under $0.05$.
A calculated negative BAC means all alcohol has been processed, so the actual BAC is $0.000$.
steps: Select the male or female BAC formula
Substitute the values for drinks, hours, and mass
Evaluate or solve for the unknown quantity

foundation.question_text:
A male weighing $75\text{ kg}$ consumes $4$ standard drinks in $2\text{ hours}$.
Use $\text{BAC}_{\text{male}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$ to calculate his estimated BAC, correct to 3 decimal places.

A male weighing $85\text{ kg}$ drinks $6$ standard drinks over $3\text{ hours}$.
Calculate his estimated BAC to 3 decimal places using $\text{BAC}_{\text{male}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$.

A female weighing $60\text{ kg}$ consumes $3$ standard drinks over $2\text{ hours}$.
Use $\text{BAC}_{\text{female}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{5.5M}$ to calculate her estimated BAC, correct to 3 decimal places.

A female weighing $50\text{ kg}$ consumes $4$ standard drinks over $3\text{ hours}$.
Use $\text{BAC}_{\text{female}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{5.5M}$ to calculate her estimated BAC to 3 decimal places.

An $80\text{ kg}$ male is at a social gathering for $4\text{ hours}$.
What is the maximum number of standard drinks $N$ he can consume to keep his estimated BAC at exactly $0.05$?
Round to 2 decimal places.

A $55\text{ kg}$ female drinks over a period of $3\text{ hours}$.
Calculate the number of standard drinks $N$ that results in an estimated BAC of exactly $0.05$.
Round to 2 decimal places.

A $70\text{ kg}$ male and a $70\text{ kg}$ female both consume $3$ standard drinks over $2\text{ hours}$.
Calculate the difference between their estimated BAC values, correct to 3 decimal places.

development.question_text:
A $92\text{ kg}$ male consumes $7$ standard drinks between $7{:}00\text{ pm}$ and $11{:}30\text{ pm}$ ($4.5\text{ hours}$).
Calculate his estimated BAC at $11{:}30\text{ pm}$, correct to 3 decimal places.

A $64\text{ kg}$ female consumes $5$ standard drinks over $3.5\text{ hours}$.
Calculate her estimated BAC to 3 decimal places and state whether she is legally permitted to drive on an unrestricted licence (limit $0.05$).
development.solution_text:
$\text{BAC}_{\text{female}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{5.5M}$
$= \dfrac{10(5) - 7.5(3.5)}{5.5(64)}$
$= \dfrac{50 - 26.25}{352}$
$= \dfrac{23.75}{352}$
$\approx 0.067$
Since $0.067 > 0.05$, she is not legally permitted to drive.

development.question_text:
A $78\text{ kg}$ male consumes $5$ standard drinks.
Calculate the number of hours $H$ he must spend drinking for his estimated BAC to be $0.02$, correct to 1 decimal place.

A $58\text{ kg}$ female drinks $4$ standard drinks.
Calculate the minimum duration of drinking $H$ in hours (to 1 decimal place) so that her estimated BAC does not exceed $0.05$.

A $100\text{ kg}$ male is drinking over a $6\text{-hour}$ period.
What is the maximum whole number of standard drinks he can consume to ensure his estimated BAC stays strictly below the legal driving limit of $0.05$?
development.solution_text:
$\text{BAC}_{\text{male}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$
$0.05 = \dfrac{10N - 7.5(6)}{6.8(100)}$
$0.05 = \dfrac{10N - 45}{680}$
$34 = 10N - 45$
$10N = 79$
$N = 7.9$
The maximum whole number of drinks is $7$.

development.question_text:
Sarah ($52\text{ kg}$) and Priya ($68\text{ kg}$) are both females who each consume $3$ standard drinks over $2\text{ hours}$.
Calculate how much higher Sarah's estimated BAC is compared to Priya's, correct to 3 decimal places.

A $56\text{ kg}$ female drinks $3$ standard drinks over $4\text{ hours}$.
Calculate her estimated BAC to 3 decimal places.

mastery.question_text:
A $62\text{ kg}$ female driver on an unrestricted licence drinks $2$ craft beers (each $1.8$ standard drinks) between $6{:}00\text{ pm}$ and $10{:}00\text{ pm}$.
She considers drinking an additional glass of wine ($1.4$ standard drinks) at $10{:}00\text{ pm}$.
Determine by calculation whether consuming this third drink will cause her estimated BAC at $10{:}00\text{ pm}$ to exceed the legal limit of $0.05$.
mastery.solution_text:
Total drinks: $N = 2(1.8) + 1.4 = 5.0$
$\text{BAC}_{\text{female}} = \dfrac{10(5) - 7.5(4)}{5.5(62)}$
$= \dfrac{50 - 30}{341}$
$= \dfrac{20}{341}$
$\approx 0.059$
Since $0.059 > 0.05$, consuming the drink will cause her BAC to exceed the legal limit.

mastery.question_text:
Liam ($82\text{ kg}$ male) and Chloe ($54\text{ kg}$ female) attend a $3\text{-hour}$ dinner.
Liam consumes $5$ standard drinks and Chloe consumes $3$ standard drinks.
Determine by calculation who has the higher estimated BAC at the end of the dinner, and find the difference to 3 decimal places.
mastery.solution_text:
$\text{BAC}_{\text{Liam}} = \dfrac{10(5) - 7.5(3)}{6.8(82)} = \dfrac{27.5}{557.6} \approx 0.0493$
$\text{BAC}_{\text{Chloe}} = \dfrac{10(3) - 7.5(3)}{5.5(54)} = \dfrac{7.5}{297} \approx 0.0253$
Liam has the higher estimated BAC.
$\text{Difference} = 0.0493 - 0.0253$
$= 0.0240$
$\approx 0.024$

mastery.question_text:
A $74\text{ kg}$ male consumed $6$ standard drinks starting at $8{:}00\text{ pm}$.
Calculate the minimum number of hours of drinking $H$ required for his BAC to fall to $0.03$ (correct to 1 decimal place), and, using the unrounded value of $H$, state the earliest clock time this occurs to the nearest minute.
